Prolongation of distal motor latency and/or distal peak sensory latency are signs of conduction delay or slowing, which is the mildest degree of neuropathy. The degree of slowing (how prolonged the measured latency, or how slow the calculated conduction veloc-ity) has little or no correlation with symptom sever-ity and no correlation with the severity of clinical signs, such as motor weakness or static large-fiber sensory loss. Distal latencies that are more than 1 millisecond beyond normal are more likely to reflect significant slowing, and less likely to represent false-positive tests. If either motor weakness or sensory loss is present on examination, substantial amounts of at least conduction block (moderate neuropathy), and usually actual axon loss (severe neuropathy), or a combination of both must be present on nerve con-duction testing.

In a case in which an examiner finds either sensory loss or neurologic strength loss on physical exam and yet the nerve conduction studies are either normal or show only conduction delay, logically, either the physical examination or the nerve conduction testing is incorrect. It may be appropriate to repeat the phys-ical examination by the same or a different examiner and/or to repeat the nerve conduction testing by an appropriately trained physician, which could include consideration of a physician with certification by the American Association of Neuromuscular and Electrodiagnostic Medicine (www.aanem.org).

Impairment Rating

The diagnosis of a focal neuropathy syndrome must be documented by sensory and motor nerve con-duction studies and/or needle EMG in order to be ratable as impairment, using this section. If nerve conduction testing has not been performed or does not meet this section’s diagnostic criteria, there is no ratable impairment from this section. These cases

may still be rated in Section 15.2, Diagnosis-Based Impairment, and with the appropriate regional grid, using the diagnosis of nonspecific hand, wrist, or elbow pain, depending on the affected region.

Threshold values for latency and conduction velocity for specific nerves are provided in Appendix 15-B. The values necessary to qualify for a diagnosis of a specific focal nerve compromise are conservative. The criteria in Appendix 15-B must be met to make the diagnosis of focal neuropathy for impairment rating purposes. In nerve conduction testing there are no universally accepted definitions of “normal” for latencies. The definitions of abnormal nerve conduction studies stated in this section are for impairment rating purposes and have been chosen to minimize the number of false-positive nerve conduction tests. Physicians may choose to use different values when diagnosing focal nerve compromise for treatment purposes.

If test findings are normal or nondiagnostic, the diagnosis is class 0 and the final rating will be class 0 for nerve entrapment (0% upper extremity impair-ment), regardless of the grade chosen for history and physical findings, and/or functional scale score. Test findings are the “key factor” for determining impair-ment in this section. The individual may, alterna-tively, be rated for impairment by Section 15.2 using the appropriate class for nonspecific hand pain.

The Functional Scale is based on the QuickDash, as described in Appendix 15-A. Descriptions of the grade modifiers for physical findings and test find-ings follows:

Physical Findings. Selection of the grade modifier for physical findings is based on documentation of significant objective sensory and motor findings. Decreased sensation means decreased 2-point dis-crimination (greater than 6 mm) for compression involving the median or ulnar nerve, or loss of sharp vs dull recognition for the rare compromise of the radial nerve. Atrophy is defined as clearly recognized neurologic atrophy (not disuse atrophy) of muscle innervated distal to the focal compromise. Thus, dis-use atrophy from thumb carpal metacarpal joint osteo-arthritis is not a “physical finding” for the purposes of calculating impairment related to focal compression. Atrophy should be recognizable by other examiners. Pain caused by or worsened during strength testing invalidates that part of the examination.

To qualify for class 3 by physical findings, there should be constant numbness (history), and no pro-tective sensation (no sharp vs dull recognition), and for the median or ulnar nerve 2-point discrimination of 16 mm or greater. There must also be grade 3 or less motor function, or a history of a surgical tendon

transfer to restore function. This is almost never seen in peripheral nerve entrapment.

Test Findings. Normal electrodiagnostic tests fail to meet the definitions necessary to permit a diagnosis of focal nerve compromise for the purpose of impair-ment rating (Appendix 15-B). Electromyographers use different, nonstandardized definitions of normal. A physician may for treatment purposes, choose to accept an electromyographer’s report interpreting a study as abnormal and consistent with focal neuropathy. However, unless the study meets the criteria listed in Appendix 15-B, it is considered a normal study for the purpose of impairment rating. The interpretation of findings for specific entrapment syndromes is provided in Appendix 15-B, Electrodiagnostic Evaluation of Entrapment Syndromes.

Conduction delay is defined as a significantly prolonged distal peak sensory and/or motor latency. It is measured by distal latencies (milliseconds) and conduction velocity calculations (meters per second). Latencies and conduction velocities that are slower than those in Appendix 15-B qualify as conduction delay for the purpose of impairment rating. Upper limb temperature must be stated in the report and must be at least 32°C.

Conduction block is measured by the amplitude (voltage) of the motor, sensory, or mixed nerve response. Stimulation proximal to the nerve compro-mise site results in a decreased amplitude recorded distal to the compromise (motor testing or anti-dromic sensory testing). With orthodromic sensory testing, stimulation distal to the compromised site results in a decrease in amplitude recorded proximal to the site of compromise. For purely sensory nerves, the SNAP amplitude must be used. For mixed motor and sensory nerves, the CMAP is used preferentially for impairment rating purposes; the lower voltage sensory amplitudes are harder to record and are more influenced by technical factors during testing.

Axon loss is documented by the needle EMG and/or nerve conduction studies. Recent and/or ongoing axon death (axonotmesis) is reflected in positive waves and fibrillation potentials in muscles innervated by the involved nerve. Chronic axon loss is documented by high-amplitude motor units and decreased motor unit recruitment. Axon loss may also be demonstrated by nerve conduction testing. A significantly low ampli-tude recorded distal to the site of compromise, with both stimulation proximal to the site and stimulation distal to the site is consistent with axon loss.

In an individual who has not had surgical treatment, a finding of high-amplitude polyphasic motor unit potentials on the needle EMG and normal distal

latencies for the nerve supplying that muscle sug-gests misinterpretation of the potentials seen on EMG. It is, therefore, not sufficient for the diagnosis of a focal neuropathy syndrome for the purpose of impairment rating.

Very mild nerve entrapments do exist and may fail to meet the Guides’ criteria for impairment related to nerve entrapment diagnosis. Similarly, although real symptoms exist in tension pattern headache, dysmen-orrhea, irritable bowel syndrome, and fibromyalgia syndrome, these conditions do not typically rise to the level of ratable impairment.

The diagnosis of severe neuropathy is made based on appropriate symptoms, a nerve conduction study compatible with at least major conduction block if not actual axon loss, and, more importantly, the pres-ence of positive clinical findings on neurologic exam (neurologic weakness or atrophy, and decreased 2-point discrimination or loss of sharp vs dull dis-crimination). The electrodiagnostic tests must meet the definition of at least conduction block and almost always will meet the definition of axon loss if the sensory exam is abnormal or if there is neurologic motor weakness present on examination.

Severe motor neuropathy (axon loss) must also be documented by needle EMG.

It is critical to understand that there is no correlation between the severity of conduction delay on nerve conduction velocity testing (latencies) and the sever-ity of either symptoms or, more importantly, the impairment rating. In other words, how “mild” the mild neuropathy is does not directly correlate with either symptoms or ADL performance. Moderate (conduction block) or severe (axon loss) neuropathy should also be documented by loss of amplitude (voltage) on nerve conduction testing.

If multiple nerve conduction tests have been per-formed, the most recent preoperative test should gen-erally be used. If the results of the most recent study cannot be directly compared with this section’s diag-nostic criteria, and results of a prior study are easily compared with this section’s diagnostic criteria, the physician should use the results that can most easily be compared with these criteria.

If a preoperative electrodiagnostic study fails to meet this section’s definition of abnormal, but surgical complications result in a postoperative electrodiag-nostic study that meets these criteria, the individual should be rated by Section 5.4e, Peripheral Nerve and Brachial Plexus Impairment. This section should not be used for these rare cases.

In the presence of CRPS II (causalgia) associated with either focal neuropathy or surgical treatment of focal neuropathy, the impairment is evaluated according to the principles of CRPS II. The diag-nostic criteria specified in Section 15.5 must be met, and the impairment is obtained using Section 15.4e Peripheral Nerve and Brachial Plexus Impairment.

Maximum Medical Improvement

Postoperatively, a sufficient amount of time for opti-mal physiologic recovery and rehabilitation should have elapsed before an individual is considered to be at MMI and to qualify for a permanent impair-ment rating. Factors affecting nerve recovery in focal neuropathy lesions include the severity of nerve fiber pathology, the level of injury, the presence and dura-tion of compression (if present), and the status of the end organs. Sensory function usually returns before motor function.

Lesions at the wrist may take 6 to 9 months for maximal recovery of nerve function, and more proximal focal axon loss lesions may take 1 to 2 years for maximal recovery. An advancing Tinel sign can be monitored and is a good prognostic sign. Grip strength may continue to gradually improve for up to 2 years following carpal tunnel release; however, the rating need not be delayed for this finding.

Although maximal recovery of nerve function may take up to 2 years, the individual can be considered at MMI when no additional improvement is likely to occur and when no specific medical intervention is necessary. The evaluator may consider the individual at MMI and calculate the impairment rating before the 9-month to 2-year time frame if, after surgery, the condition is stable for 2 consecutive office visits spaced at least 1 month apart.

If the physician finds that the clinical status of the individual is more severe than suggested by electro-diagnostic studies that are more than 1 year old, a current electrodiagnostic study may be appropriate. The examiner may defer rating the impairment until a current nerve conduction test is performed.

Permanent impairment for focal neuropathy may be calculated even when the patient has declined sur-gery. However, the functional score should reflect symptoms insufficiently severe to warrant surgery. If an individual has a QuickDASH functional score greater than 60, and chooses not to have surgery, the examiner should suspect symptom magnification on the QuickDASH questionnaire. Since entrapments typically produce numbness as the dominant symp-tom, and not pain, the QuickDASH must be used for functional assessment (the visual analog pain scale,

or VAPS, may not be used, since it measures pain). If symptom magnification is not present, a psychia-trist or psychologist may be consulted to document a phobia relating to surgical treatment. If an individual who chooses not to have surgical treatment is rated “at MMI,” the physician should comment in the report that the neuropathy may change with time, and that in the future the impairment rating may be different.

Postoperative Electrodiagnostics

Postoperative nerve conduction studies are not required to rate impairment for focal nerve com-promise syndromes. Significant improvement in nerve conduction studies usually occurs. Some of the improvement is almost immediate, and some occurs over months. Many individuals recover and are asymptomatic, but nerve conduction testing still detects minor slowing (prolonged latencies). Whether or not the nerve conduction tests recover to normal after surgical or nonsurgical treatment does not influence the impairment rating. The preopera-tive electrodiagnostic test should be used in the impairment rating unless postoperative studies were done for a clinical indication of failure to improve with surgery and the postoperative study is clearly worse than the preoperative electrodiagnostic study. In this rare case the postoperative study is used in this section.

Persistence of symptoms and failure of preoperative nerve conduction studies to improve after surgery suggests that either the diagnosis was incorrect (peripheral neuropathy is present and not focal neuropathy) or that surgical decompression did not result in improved nerve function. Nerve decompres-sion may have been incomplete, or the nerve may have been so severely compromised that it could not recover. Further evaluation by both an electromyog-rapher certified by the American Association of Neuromuscular and Electrodiagnostic Medicine and a hand surgeon is indicated in these rare cases.

Multiple Simultaneous Neuropathies

Multiple, concurrent focal nerve compromise syn-dromes in the same upper limb are being diagnosed more frequently. Individual risk factors such as pre-existing diabetic peripheral neuropathy and heredi-tary generalized peripheral neuropathy likely play a role in persons who present with simultaneous carpal tunnel syndrome and ulnar neuropathy at the elbow. Both impairments may be rated using this section, and in this section only, the functional scale would apply to each diagnosis. The nerve qualifying for the larger impairment is given the full impairment. The nerve qualifying for the smaller impairment is

rated at 50% (one-half) of the impairment listed in Table 15-23, Entrapment/Compression Neuropathy Impairment. The impairments are then combined. In the event that the rating ends in .5%, it should be rounded to the next integer. This method considers the fact that both ratings incorporate symptoms and the functional scale. Nerve conduction testing of the upper limbs can clarify the role of generalized peripheral nerve disease and is especially helpful in jurisdictions that require apportionment between systemic disease and work activity.

If 3 focal neuropathies are diagnosed and supported by the requirements of inclusion, the third (or small-est impairment) is not rated. If more than 3 diagnos-able focal neuropathies are identified and supported by the requirements of inclusion, this section should not be used. The peripheral neuropathy section of the neurology chapter should be used, as in these cases almost always the principal problem is a general-ized peripheral neuropathy (medical disease) and not related to occupational or avocational activities. In jurisdictions that require apportionment, the majority of causation for the individual with 3 or more simul-taneous focal nerve neuropathies should be appor-tioned to the medical disease and not to occupation.

Rating Process

To rate the impairment for focal nerve compro-mise, use Table 15-23, Entrapment/Compression Neuropathy Impairment. Grade modifiers are described for test findings, history, and physical findings. If test findings are grade modifier 0 (ie, electrodiagnostic testing is normal or does not meet standards), do not use this section. The QuickDASH is used to further modify the grade and to choose the appropriate numerical impairment rating.

1. Determine the appropriate grade modifier for test findings, history (symptoms), and physical findings. Determine the average value for these 3 modifiers using the associated number for each grade; for example, grade 0 has a value of 0 and grade 1 has a value of 1. Round that aver-age value to the nearest integer to determine the average grade. For example, if grade modifiers are grade 1 for history, grade 2 for physical find-ings, and grade 1 for tests findings, add the cor-responding numerical values: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. Then 4 divided by 3 is 1.33, which rounds to 1, so grade 1 is the final rating category.

General Considerations for Test Results: A study result may be considered abnormal for treatment purposes, but, for impairment rating purposes, elec-trodiagnostic studies that do not meet the specified criteria are considered normal, and the individual is either placed in grade 0 by test findings, and has no impairment, or is rated as applicable according to DBI.

In cases in which surgical decompression has been performed, if the preoperative study fails to meet the specified criteria, this section cannot be used to rate the impairment. The DBI should be used for those cases. Such individuals are placed in class 0 for test findings according to Table 15-23, Entrapment/ Compression Neuropathy Impairment, and are not ratable by this section.

Individuals whose test results describe normal laten-cies, but in whom “inching” results in detection of a conduction delay and/or a change in amplitude in 1 or a few 1-cm segments of a nerve, are consid-ered to have a normal nerve conduction study result for impairment rating purposes. The interpreta-tion of findings for specific entrapment syndromes is provided in Appendix 15-B, Electrodiagnostic Evaluation of Entrapment Syndromes.

EXAMPLE 15-18:CARPAL TUNNEL SYNDROME

Subject: 55-year-old woman.

History: Insidious onset of right-side symptoms consistent with carpal tunnel syndrome. Diagnosis confirmed electrodiagnostically and underwent car-pal tunnel release two years ago. Symptoms stable for over a year. Determined administratively to be work-related.

Current Symptoms: Complaints of significant intermittent problems with numbness and discom-

fort; however, able to perform all activities of daily living, despite symptoms.

Functional Assessment: QuickDASH score is 14.

Physical Exam: Normal, including sensory examina-tion (2 point and monofilament testing), focal muscle testing and range of motion. Well-healed scar.

Clinical Studies: Electrodiagnostic studies pre-operatively revealed mild sensory and motor conduction delays of the right median nerve.

Diagnosis: Carpal tunnel syndrome, s/p carpal tunnel release

Impairment Rating: The diagnosis of carpal tun-nel syndrome was confirmed electrodiagnostically and the patient is at maximal medical improve-ment. Rating is based on Table 15-23, Entrapment/ Compression Neuropathy. Testing findings are grade modifier 1 (conduction delay), history is grade modifier 2 (significant intermittent symptoms), and physical findings are grade modifier 1 (normal). The grade modifiers total 4 (1+2+1) and average 1.33. Therefore, grade modifier 1 is selected with a default of 2% UEI; however, the QuickDASH is 14 in the normal range, therefore, the lowest UEI for that grade modifier is selected, i.e. 1% UEI which is equivalent to 1% hand impairment or 1% WPI.

EXAMPLE 15-19: MULTIPLE ENTRAPMENTS

Subject: 40-year-old man.

History: Insidious onset of right-side symptoms diagnosed as right carpal tunnel syndrome and right ulnar syndrome. Diagnoses confirmed electrodiag-nostically and underwent carpal tunnel and ulnar release eighteen months ago. Symptoms stable for four months. Determined administratively to be work-related.

Current Symptoms: Reports minimal problems in the distribution of the median nerve, basically mild intermittent paresthesias, however no true numb-ness. In the distribution of the ulnar nerve continues to have significant complaints of numbness that are essentially constant. He is able to perform all activi-ties of daily living, despite symptoms. Feels right hand is weaker than it was in the past.

Functional Assessment: QuickDASH score is 32.

Physical Exam: Diminished sensibility in the distri-bution of the ulnar nerve (monofilament testing 3.61 grams); however two point discrimination normal (5 mm). Normal sensory assessment of median nerve. Motor examination normal. Range of motion normal.

Clinical Studies: Electrodiagnostic studies pre-operatively revealed mild sensory and motor conduc-tion delays of the right median nerve and condution block of the right ulnar nerve at the elbow.

Diagnosis: Carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve entrapment) and cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar neu-ropathy), s/p release.

Impairment Rating: The diagnosis of median nerve and ulnar nerve entrapment was confirmed electro-diagnostically and the patient is at maximal medi-cal improvement. Rating is based on Table 15-23, Entrapment/Compression Neuropathy.

For median nerve entrapment, testing findings are grade modifier 1 (conduction delay), history is grade modifier 1 (mild intermittent symptoms), and physi-cal findings are grade modifier 1 (normal). The grade modifiers total 3 (1 + 1 + 1) and average 1. Therefore, grade modifier 1 is selected with a default of 2% UEI. The QuickDASH is 32 (mild) and this results in assignment of the mid-range default value of 2% UEI for the median nerve.

For ulnar nerve entrapment, test findings are grade modifier 2 (conduction block), history is constant symptoms, but only conduction block is present on nerve conduction testing, so grade 2 is the highest permitted grade. Physical findings are grade modi-fier 2 (decreased sensation). The grade modifiers total 6 (2 + 2 + 2) and average 2. Therefore, grade modifier 2 is selected with a default of 5% UEI. The QuickDASH is 32 (mild), therefore, for grade modi-fier the lowest value for that grade is selected and the impairment is 4% UEI for the ulnar nerve.

With multiple entrapments the nerve qualifying for the larger impairment is given the full impairment, ie, the ulnar nerve with 4% UEI. This is combined with 50% of the rating of the second nerve, the median nerve that was rated at 2% UEI. The combined value of 4% UEI and 1% UEI (50% of 2% UEI) results in 5% UEI.

15.5 Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Impairment

Complex regional pain syndrome is a challenging and controversial concept. It is difficult to diagnose accurately, and epidemiological studies indicate that most such diagnoses are made within a workers’ compensation context. Therefore, this is a particu-larly challenging diagnosis to rate. The hallmark of this condition is a characteristic burning pain that is present without stimulation or movement, that occurs

beyond the territory of a single peripheral nerve, and that is disproportionate to any suspected inciting event. The pain is associated with specific clinical findings, including signs of vasomotor and sudomo-tor dysfunction and, later, trophic changes of all tis-sues from skin to bone.

The International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) created the diagnoses of CRPS type I to replace the diagnosis of RSD, and CRPS type II to replace causalgia. Historically, sympathetic nervous system dysfunction was thought to be a cause of symptoms, and the term RSD reflects that. Causalgia was considered similar to RSD except it followed an unambiguous lesion of a peripheral nerve, either a major mixed nerve in the proximal extremity (major causalgia) or of a purely sensory branch more dis-tally (minor causalgia). Currently, CRPS I is consid-ered when clinically appropriate signs and symptoms are present in the limb without nerve injury, and CRPS II is considered when appropriate signs and symptoms are present in the clinical setting of an unambiguous injury to a specific peripheral nerve.

Since a subjective complaint of pain is the hallmark of this diagnosis, and since all of the associated physical signs and radiologic findings can be the result of disuse, an extensive differential diagnostic process is necessary. Differential diagnoses that must be ruled out include disuse atrophy, unrec-ognized general medical problems, somatoform disorders, factitious disorder, and malingering. A diagnosis of CRPS may be excluded in the presence of any of these conditions, or any other conditions which could account for the presentation. This exclu-sion is necessary due to the general lack of scientific validity for the concept of CRPS, and due to the reported extreme rarity of CRPS (any of the differ-entials would be far more probable).

Because accurate diagnosis of CRPS is difficult, the diagnostic approach should be conservative, and sup-ported by objective findings. The diagnosis of CRPS has not been scientifically validated as representing a specific and discrete health condition. The diagnostic process is itself unreliable, as competing diagnostic protocols and definitions are continuously being introduced and utilized. There is no gold standard diagnostic feature which reliably distinguishes the diagnosis of CRPS from presentations that clearly are not CRPS. Scientific findings have actually indicated that whenever this diagnosis is made, it is probably incorrect. A diagnosis of CRPS may create a dilemma for the evaluator with regard to a specific injury. Specifically, a lack of proportionality between a clinical presentation and any suspected inciting event is inherent to the concept of CRPS. Therefore,

an evaluator must determine if there is relationship between CRPS and the injury in question.

Complex regional pain syndrome may be rated only when: (1) the diagnosis is confirmed by objective parameters (specified later in this section), (2) the diagnosis has been present for at least 1 year (to ensure accuracy of the diagnosis and to permit adequate time to achieve MMI), (3) the diagnosis has been verified by more than 1 physician, and (4) a comprehensive differential diagnostic process (which may include psychological evaluation and psychologi-cal testing) has clearly ruled out all other differential diagnoses. Emphasis is placed on the differential diagnostic process because accurate diagnosis of CRPS is difficult and because even objective findings have been demonstrated to lack diagnostic validity.

The taxonomy and criteria, which were adopted by the IASP Committee for Classification of Chronic Pain of the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP), have contributed to progress in understand-ing the syndrome. These substantial efforts finally provided standardized diagnostic criteria, improved clinical communication and homogeneity of research, and provided the promise of results that could be com-pared across studies. These criteria have been exam-ined both in terms of external and internal validation. The IASP criteria, while sensitive, lack specificity, that is, they would identify patients as having CRPS when they do not. As a result of validation studies, proposed modified research diagnostic criteria were developed. A formal international consensus resulted in the criteria shown in Table 15-24.

Signs are objective evidence of disease perceptible to the examiner, as opposed to symptoms, which are subjective sensations of the individual. The examiner should provide objective evidence of the reported findings (eg, photographic documentation, tempera-ture measurements) whenever possible. The presence or absence of the objective factors shown in Table 15-25 should be noted.

In CRPS I, neither the initiating causative factor nor the symptoms involve a specific peripheral nerve structure; therefore, impairment is based on Table 15-26, Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (Type I). In CRPS II a specific sensory or mixed nerve struc-ture is involved; therefore, the rating is based on Table 15-21 Peripheral Nerve Impairment – Upper Extremity Impairments. With CRPS II the sever-ity of CRPS is first determined using Table 15-26 Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (Type 1).

The steps in assessing CRPS type 1 impairment are as follows:

1. Determine if CRPS is a ratable diagnosis—that the diagnosis has been confirmed (Table 15-24 Diagnostic Criteria for Complex Regional Pain Syndrome), the diagnosis has been present for at least 1 year, the diagnosis has been verified by more than 1 physician, and a comprehensive dif-ferential diagnostic process has clearly ruled out all other differential diagnoses.

2. Determine the number of objective diagnostic criteria points (Table 15-25 Objective Diagnostic Criteria Points for Complex Regional Pain Syndrome).

3. Assess adjustment factors, as described in Section 15.3.

4. The classification of severity is based on the number of objective diagnostic criteria points and assessment of adjustment factors, as described in Section 15.3. A minimum of 4 points is required for a class 1 rating, 6 points for a class 2 rating, and 8 points for a class 3 or 4 rating. If there are 3 points or less, the rating for pain complaints may be based on Chapter 3, Pain, as applicable.

5. Using Table 15-7 Functional History Adjustment Modification, Table 15-8 Physical Examination Adjustment Modification, and Table 15-9 Clinical Studies Adjustment Modification, iden-tify the grade modifier number for each adjust-ment factor that is determined to be reliable. The process differs from that used for DBIs. Average the grade modifier numbers and use this information to define the class number in Table 15-26 Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (Type

1) – Upper Extremity Impairments. If that class number is not supported by the objective diag-nostic criteria points, the highest class specified by those points is selected. For example, if an individual has grade modifiers that ultimately resulted in assignment to class 2 but the objective diagnostic criteria points were only 4, the indi-vidual would be assigned to class 1. Using clini-cal judgment, select the appropriate grade within the class. Since the adjustment factors are used to define the class, they cannot be used to determine the grade within the class. The physician may use clinical judgment to decrease or increase the grade within the assigned class and must explain in detail the rationale for any adjustments.

The rating for CRPS is a “stand alone” approach. If impairment is assigned for CRPS, no additional impairment is assigned for pain from Chapter 3, nor is the CRPS impairment combined with any other approach for the same extremity from this chapter.

CLASS 3 26% to 49% Impairment of the Upper Extremity

EXAMPLE 15-20: COMPLEX REGIONAL PAIN SYNDROME, TYPE 1

Subject: 32-year-old man.

History: Two years ago sustained blunt trauma to his right arm, and subsequently developed problems consistent with complex regional pain syndrome. He underwent extensive diagnostic evaluation, both physical and psychological, and no other diagnoses were identified. Despite appropriate therapy he con-tinues to have significant difficulties.

Current Symptoms: Reports significant problems with pain, particularly with touch, and that the arm will swell, change colors, and feel cool. He has noted that motion and strength are decreased. Able to per-form self-care activities, however with significant difficulty and requires assistance for some activities.

Functional Assessment: QuickDASH score is 73.

Physical Exam: Makes minimal use of right upper limb, maintaining it at his side. Complains of sig-nificant tenderness on palpation particularly over the forearm. The limb is edematous, mottled and feels cool; the opposite side is normal. Skin texture is smooth and nonelastic. Hair on right forearm is fine compared to the opposite side. There is a mild decrease in elbow, wrist, and hand motion. Weakness due to pain is present. The findings were consistent through out the visit.

Clinical Studies: Radiographs reveal moderately severe trophic bone changes and bone scan is consis-tent with CRPS.

Differential Diagnosis: A comprehensive medical investigation, including a review of the examinee’s records from his entire life, failed to reveal any general medical differentials. A comprehensive psychological evaluation, including a review of the examinee’s records from his entire life, diagnostic evaluation in accordance with the American Psychiatric Association’s diagnostic manual (Axes I and II), collateral input, and scientifically credible psychological testing, failed to reveal any psychologi-cal diagnoses.

Work-relatedness Considerations: Administratively it was determined that his complex regional pain syn-drome was attributable to the injury two years prior.

Diagnosis: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), Type 1.

15.6 Amputation Impairment

Impairment for amputation is based on the level of the amputation, with adjustment for proximal prob-lems, and adjustment for functional history, physi-cal examination, and clinical studies. Impairment ratings for upper limb amputation increase with progressively shorter stumps, and reach 70% of the whole person for a scapulothoracic (forequarter) amputation. Impairments that may be rated and combined to the amputation impairment include impairments for loss of motion in retained joints, impairments for neurologic loss in the retained por-tion of the limb, and DBIs of the residual stump.

The upper limb is considered as a unit of the whole person and is divided into thumb, fingers, hand, wrist, elbow, and shoulder. From distal to proximal, each anatomic unit is given a relative value to the

next larger unit, and eventually, the whole person. By understanding the appropriate percent impair-ment of each anatomic unit, impairments can be converted sequentially to hand, upper limb, and whole person by using Table 15-11 and Table 15-12. These impairments are shown in Tables 15-27 and 15-28, and in Figures 15-9 through 15-12.

If a limb has both an amputation and a nerve injury, do not rate the nerve injury for loss of sensation in the amputated part.

15.6a Amputation of Thumb/Finger

Principles

The digits represent 5 coordinated units, which contribute unequally to hand function. To avoid con-fusion, digits are named rather than numbered as fol-lows: thumb, index, middle, ring, and little. Each digit is given a relative value to the entire hand as follows:

• Thumb: 40%.

• Index and middle fingers: 20% each.

• Ring and little fingers: 10% each.

These values are listed in Figure 15-10 and Table 15-27.

Amputation through each joint level of a digit is given a relative value of loss to the entire digit as follows:

Thumb (Figure 15-10 and Table 15-28):

• Interphalangeal (IP) joint: 50% of thumb.

• Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint: 100% of thumb.

Finger (Figure 15-10 and Table 15-28):

• Distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint: 45% of finger.

• Proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint: 80% of finger.

• Metacarpophalangeal joint: 100% of finger.

For amputations of 1 or more digits, Figures 15-11 and 15-12 easily permit an impairment rating based on the retained length of the digit.

Amputation of the thumb and all fingers at the MCP joints removes the most essential parts of the hand and is considered 100% impairment of the hand or 90% impairment of the upper limb, as in Figure 15-9 and Table 15-28. This 90% upper limb impairment is equivalent to a 54% whole person impairment, as seen in Figure 15-9 and Table 15-28.

Impairment is determined individually for each amputation of thumb/fingers/hand and impairments of the digits are converted to hand impairments using Table 15-12. The hand impairments are added; however, the total hand impairment cannot exceed 100%. Hand impairment can then be converted to an upper limb impairment, and to whole person impair-ment by using Table 15-11.

EXAMPLE 15-21: AMPUTATION OF FINGERS

Subject: 35-year-old woman.

History: The patient was working in an assembly line and sustained an amputation of the index finger and middle finger through the PIP joint of each of these fingers. During the evaluation, the fingers are well healed and there is retained motion at the MCP joints.

Functional Assessment: Not obtained.

Physical Exam: Well-healed stumps at the index and middle finger with no tenderness of the healed scars or digital neuromas.

Clinical Studies: Confirm amputation levels.

Diagnosis: Amputation at the PIP joint of index and middle finger.

Impairment Rating: Per Table 15-28, amputation at the PIP joint of the index finger is rated at 16% of the hand and amputation of the middle finger is rated at 16% of the hand. Hand impairments are added and total 32% of the hand. This equates to 29% UEI or 17% WPI.

15.6b Amputation of Hand Metacarpals (Proximal to Metacarpophalangeal Joint) or Through the Wrist

Amputations of the thumb at levels proximal to the MCP joint (through the metacarpal bone) are con-sidered to result in a greater severity of impairment than amputation at the MCP joint level. These ampu-tations remove part of the palm, and thus decrease function. For amputations through the thumb meta-carpal, the impairments are as follows:

• Amputation through the thumb MCP joint is a 40% impairment of the hand or a 36% impair-ment of the upper limb.

• Amputation at the middle of the thumb metacar-pal is a 41% impairment of the hand or a 37% impairment of the upper limb.

• Amputation at the CMC joint represents a 42% impairment of the hand or a 38% impairment of the upper limb.

For amputations through 1 to 4 metacarpals, the impairments are as follows:

• Amputation at the middle half of the index or middle finger metacarpal is a 21% impairment of the hand or 19% impairment of the upper limb.

• Amputation at middle half of the ring or little fin-ger metacarpal is a 12% impairment of the hand or an 11% impairment of the upper limb.

• Amputation at the CMC joint of the index or middle finger ray is a 22% impairment of the hand or a 20% impairment of the upper limb.

• Amputation at the CMC joint of the ring or little finger ray is a 13% impairment of the hand or a 12% impairment of the upper limb.

When all 5 rays have transmetacarpal amputations, the impairments are:

• Amputation of all 5 rays at the middle of the metacarpals is a 91% upper limb impairment.

• Amputation of all 5 rays at the CMC joint is a 92% upper limb impairment.

• Amputation at the wrist (either through the radius-proximal carpal row joint or through the proximal carpal row-distal carpal row joints) is a 93% upper limb impairment.

If the total hand impairment exceeds 100% because of amputations involving all 5 digits or rays, the upper limb percentages just listed are used.

Injuries to the tip or distal phalanx of a digit can result in loss of pulp (soft-tissue padding over the bone of the distal phalanx) or the presence of tender scars that limit function. If the pulp loss is suffi-cient to qualify as an amputation by Figure 15-11 or Figure 15-12, the impairment rating for the amputa-tion is usually adequate. If the loss of pulp or a ten-der scar causes the individual to exclude (not use) the

digit in functional tasks, an additional impairment is present. In such cases, if a ratable amputation has occurred, the physician may combine an additional 10% digit impairment to the digit amputation impairment.

Digital Neuromas and Digital Nerve Injury

Amputations through digits may have residual sensory loss from associated digital nerve injury and may have a neuroma in the retained portion of the digit. Sensory loss should be documented by decreased 2-point discrimination. Loss of sensa-tion is rated by use of Figure 15-4 and Figure 15-5 to determine how much of the remaining length of the digit has sensory loss, and Table 15-16 and 15-17

ulnar digital nerve of the fifth finger; full range of motion of other fingers.

Clinical Studies: X ray confirms amputation at the middle of the fifth metacarpal.

Diagnosis: Amputation of the little finger at the middle of the fifth metacarpal with a digital neu-roma (ulnar digital nerve of the little finger).

Impairment Rating: Per Figure 15-10, an amputa-tion through the metacarpal shaft of the little finger rates a 12% impairment of the hand. A 10% impair-ment of the digit can be combined for the symptom-atic digital neuroma; this is first converted to hand using Table 15-12 resulting in 1% hand impairment. The 12% hand impairment due to amputation and the 1% hand impairment associated with the neu-roma results in a combined 13% hand impairment which converts to 12% UEI or 7% WPI.

Comment: An alternative is to not rate the neuroma, but rather to rate the amputation from Table 15-29 with adjustments.

Amputations With Range of Motion Loss

Any impairment resulting from lost of or restricted motion of proximal joints is evaluated according to Section 15.7, Range of Motion Impairment. For each functional unit, the impairment rating cannot exceed 100% of the unit.

For example, if a digit has an amputation through the middle phalanx, loss of motion at the PIP and/or MCP joint or joints, and sensory loss in the retained portion of the digit, the impairments for each of the 3 prob-lems are calculated and combined. The final impair-ment for the digit cannot exceed 100% of the digit. Similarly, hand impairments determined by adding impairments for amputation, loss of motion, and neu-rologic loss cannot exceed 100% of the hand. Upper extremity impairments determined by combining impairments for amputation, loss of motion, and neu-rologic loss cannot exceed 100% of the upper extremity.

15.6e Final Amputation Rating

Use the process described above to determine the impairment due to the level of amputation and also use of Table 15-29. In most circumstances the impairment is based on the level of the amputa-tion with adjustment for proximal problems, and on functional history, physical examination, and clini-cal studies. The default middle grade value (C) and values to the left are consistent with the impairment values presented in this section. It is not possible to decrease impairment below the value associated with the amputation level; however, proximal prob-lems may increase the impairment (ie, may result

in assignment to grade D or grade E). These adjust-ments are performed as outlined in Section 15.3. The amputation impairment may be combined with either proximal DBIs or range of motion impair-ments; they cannot be combined with both since this is duplicative. If combined with range of motion the Table 15-29 midrange default is used unless there are significant other adjustment factors that should be considered. If an amputation is only to a digit and the resulting impairment is to be expressed at the digit level, the processes described above will allow a more precise calculation of the digit impairment.

EXAMPLE 15-23: AMPUTATION WITH RANGE OF MOTION LOSS

Subject: 44-year-old man.

History: The patient sustained an open fracture of the distal forearm with soft-tissue loss. Chronic draining osteomyelitis developed, which was treated with an amputation. A flexion contracture of the elbow developed during treatment of the initial con-dition, and this persisted after the amputation.

Current Symptoms: The stump is not painful and the patient is able to use a below-elbow prosthesis with little difficulty; no complaints of phantom limb pain or other sensations.

Physical Exam: Well-healed stump without tender-ness; range of motion of the elbow is full in flexion, with an extension lag of 50°.

Clinical Studies: Consistent.

Diagnosis: Amputation of the forearm distal to the bicipital tuberosity of the radius with flexion con-tracture of the elbow above the amputation.

Impairment Rating: Amputation through the radius and ulna between the bicipital tuberosity of the radius and the wrist per Figure 15-9 is between 90% UEI and 95% UEI and per Table 15-28 90% to 94% UEI. Per Table 15-29, Amputation Impairment this is a Class 4 impairment with a midrange default of 92% UEI. In that the amputation is combined with the impair-ment of the upper limb, the midrange default is used. Per Table 15-33 Elbow/Forearm Range of Motion a 50°extensor lag at the elbow is 5% UEI. Combining these 2 values is still 92% UEI or 55% WPI.

15.7 Range of Motion Impairment

Range of motion determination is an essential com-ponent of upper extremity impairment ratings with a

strong historical precedent. Although the procedure may be time-consuming, valuable objective informa-tion concerning joint function can be ascertained. Surface goniometry can be carried out reliably and effectively on the joints of the extremities, so that range of motion can be objectively determined. The conventional range of motion goniometric proce-dures advocated in earlier Editions of the Guides should be followed. However, certain procedural modifications, described below, have been imple-mented to enhance simplicity and reproducibility of results, and the tables have been reformatted and simplified considerably to conform more effectively to the requisite ICF approach.

Section 15.2 Diagnosis-Based Impairments, is the method of choice for calculating impairment. Range of motion is used principally as a factor in the Adjustment Grid: Physical Examination, as explained in Section 15.3b. Some of the DBI grids refer to the range of motion section when that is the most appropriate mechanism for grading the impair-ment. This section is to be used as a stand-alone rating when other grids refer you to this section or when no other diagnosis-based sections of this chapter are applicable for impairment rating of a condition. The final impairment may be adjusted for functional history in certain circumstances. Figure 15-13, Upper Extremity Range of Motion Record, is used to record motion findings and to document impairments. Examples of the latter include burns or other severe scarring causing permanent passive and active range of motion losses, complex flexor or extension tendon or multiple tendon laceration injuries, severe crush injuries, residual compartment syndrome, or other conditions not addressed in the regional grids but having significant functional loss. Range of motion may also be used for rating in the following 2 situations:

1. For amputation ratings, deficits of motion for the remaining portion of the limb may be combined with the amputation impairment.

2. In very rare cases, severe injuries may result in passive range of motion losses qualifying for class 3 or 4 impairment. If the active range of motion impairment percentage is greater than the percentage impairment derived from the diag-nosis-based class, then the impairment is rated by range of motion as a stand-alone rating. This range of motion for the impairment may only be used if the active range of motion is within 10° of the passive range of motion measured. The active range of motion measurement is what determines the final impairment rating. Examples include complex flexor or extension tendon or multiple

tendon laceration injuries, severe crush injuries, residual compartment syndrome, or other condi-tions having significant functional loss.

15.7a Clinical Measurements of Motion

As in prior editions of the Guides, active range of motion is measured for impairment rating and takes precedence over passive range of motion. However, the 2 should be examined concurrently for the following reasons: many different factors can limit the normal range of motion of the joints of the upper extremities; limitation of active motion can be due to failure of the nerve, muscle, tendon, or effort to execute the motion. If pain is present during range of motion testing, muscle guarding may also limit motion. This guarding should be palpable. Limitation of passive motion can be from involvement of the joint itself, a fixed contracture, or the antagonistic muscle or tendon that holds back the motion because it is adherent or too short.

Active range of motion is a more sensitive indicator of joint loss of motion but is also more sensitive to symptom magnification and self-inhibition by the patient. If active motion differs significantly from passive range of motion, the examiner should note the difference and provide a pathological explana-tion (eg, abduction weakness after a rotator cuff tear prevents full motion against gravity). As in prior editions of the Guides, the examiner is permitted to disallow the rating for loss of active range of motion if there is not a patho-anatomic or physiological cor-relate, and there is suboptimal effort or symptom magnification. Sound clinical knowledge and mea-surement techniques are necessary for appropriate impairment evaluation and rating using range of motion deficits.

If the opposite extremity is neither involved nor previously injured, it must be used to define normal for that individual; any losses should be made in comparison to the opposite normal extremity.

Joint range of motion measurements are rounded to the nearest whole number ending in 0. Thus, joint motion is not recorded as 32° or as 48°, but rather as 30° and 50°, respectively. Joint motion cannot be reliably measured to the level of single degrees.

Neutral Zero Reference System

The Neutral Zero (system of goniometric reference) is used for all joint measurements, and is based on the premise of the neutral position of a joint being the zero position, as illustrated in Figure 15-14.

As illustrated in Figure 15-14, the “extended ana-tomic position” is accepted as 0° rather than 180° and the degrees of joint motion increase in the

direction the joint moves from the zero starting point. The term extension describes motion opposite to flexion. Incomplete extension from a flexed position to the neutral starting point is defined as extension lag. Extension exceeding the zero starting position, as can be seen in normal MCP, elbow, and knee joints, is referred to as hyperextension. Ankylosis refers to complete absence of motion of a joint.

For ease of notation, a plus sign (+) is used to indi-cate joint hyperextension and a minus sign (−) to indicate extension lag. These signs have no math-ematical significance. Using this notation system, a finger joint flexion contracture (limitation of passive extension) with an identical extension lag (limitation of active extension) of 10°, with active flexion to 40° would be recorded as −10° to 40°. A joint motion with 10° hyperextension and 40° flexion would be recorded as +10° to 40°.

The arc of motion represents the total number of degrees traced between the 2 extreme positions of movement in a specific plane of motion, for example, from maximum flexion to maximum extension of the PIP joint. When a joint has more than 1 plane of motion, each type of motion is referred to as a unit of motion. For example, the wrist has 2 units of motion: flexion/extension (AP or sagittal plane) and ulnar/radial deviation (lateral or coronal plane). The term functional position of a joint denotes the opti-mal or least impairing angle or angles recommended for surgical joint fusion. When a joint has more than 1 unit of motion, each separate unit is assigned a functional position. For example, the functional position of the elbow is considered to be 80° flexion and 20° pronation.

Assessing Motion

In assessing motion, the examiner should first observe what a patient can and cannot do by ask-ing him or her to move each joint of the extremity, from thumb and fingers up to the shoulder, through its full range of motion. Both extremities should be examined whenever possible, since right vs left comparisons between the affected and unaffected side are useful to help determine the “normal” baseline. Individual joints are then evaluated sepa-rately. Similarly, movements of the digits are first evaluated as a unit by having the individual make a complete fist and then extend the digits fully over several repetitions. In determining the range of motion of individual joints, the examiner must evaluate both active and passive motion. The posi-tions and techniques used to measure active range of motion are retained from the Fifth Edition, since

these are very familiar to physicians treating muscu-loskeletal disorders.

Active or voluntary motion is movement that is performed by the active contraction of the govern-ing muscles and is evaluated first. When a person has full active joint motion ( joint excursion or arc of motion), passive motion does not need to be assessed because a joint that has full active excur-sion will also have full passive range. However, if the full active joint excursion is incomplete, assisted active and/or passive motion measurements are nec-essary to evaluate the joint motion. Measurements of active motion take precedence in the Guides. The actual measured goniometer readings are rounded to end in 0 and are then recorded.

Passive motion is movement produced by an external force to evaluate the freedom and range of motion of a joint when all muscles are relaxed. Assisted active motion is the result of active muscle contraction and an external force applied to the joint; it allows for stabilization of a segment to improve the mechanical advantage of the muscles that move the joint being measured. In both cases, approximately 0.5 kg of force is applied while a seg-ment of the joint is stabilized. Joint motion may be uncomfortable but, when examined in this manner, neither active assisted nor passive range of motion measurements will cause injury to an individual. These techniques are part of traditional musculosk-eletal physical examination.

Range of motion should be measured after a “warm up,” in which the individual moves the joint through its maximum range of motion at least 3 times. The range of motion examination is then performed by recording the active measurements from 3 separate range of motion efforts.* Measurements should be rounded up or down to the nearest number end-ing in 0 (eg, 20°instead of 24° and 30° instead of 25°). All measurements should fall within 10° of the mean of these 3 measurements. The maximum observed measurement is used to determine the range of motion impairment. The examiner should compare the observed findings with other findings documented since the individual has been at MMI, to further determine the reliability of the measure-ments. It is recognized that patients may under-demonstrate their capabilities.

15.7b International Classification of Functioning Range of Motion Model

To facilitate reproducibility and to adjust to the ICF Model of impairment, the Sixth Edition of the

Guides reflects motion loss as grade modifiers, as shown in the following table.

Grade modifiers are determined by the criteria pro-vided or relative to the opposite extremity if it is nor-mal. Specific range of motion tables are provided for the thumb, fingers, wrist, elbow, and shoulder in the following sections. Each table provides a range of motion loss in degrees that places the individual into an impairment grade modifier that provides a spe-cific impairment rating. Grade modifier 4 impair-ments for ankylosis provide specific impairments based on the position of the ankylosis.

15.7c Thumb Motion

The thumb has 3 articular units: IP joint, MCP joint, and CMC joint. The actual range-of-motion measurements for each unit are recorded and the appropriate thumb impairments are identified. Because they are expressed with the same relative value of the denominator, the impairment percentages contributed by each unit are added directly. The 5 thumb functional units of motion have been assigned a relative value to the entire thumb on a 100% scale as follows:

Interphalangeal joint flexion and extension: 15%. Metacarpophalangeal joint flexion and extension: 10%. Carpometacarpal joint: 75% (radial abduction: 10%, adduction: 20%, and opposition: 45%).

Thumb Interphalangeal Joint: Flexion and Extension

The thumb IP joint motion ranges from +30° hyper-extension to 80° flexion. The functional position is 20° flexion. The relative value of this functional unit is 15% of the thumb.

1. Measure the maximum active flexion and exten-sion according to Figure 15-15 and record to the nearest 10°.

2. Using the row for IP flexion in Table 15-30, com-pare the measured greatest angle of flexion to the IP flexion ranges in each column to establish the appropriate grade modifier (and impairment per-centage if indicated). Repeat this process for IP extension.

3. Add the flexion impairment to the extension impairment to determine the total thumb impair-ment for decreased active motion of the IP joint.

4. If the IP joint is ankylosed, grade modifier 4 is used. The impairment is based on the angle of the ankylosis.

Thumb Metacarpophalangeal Joint: Flexion and Extension

The thumb MCP joint motion can range from +40° hyperextension to 60° flexion, although many normal people have no hyperextension or a slight flexion contracture. The functional position is 20° flexion. The relative value of the functional unit is 10% of the thumb.

1. Measure the maximum active flexion and extension according to Figure 15-16.

2. Using the row for MCP flexion in Table 15-30, compare the measured greatest angle of flexion to the MCP flexion ranges in each column to estab-lish the appropriate grade modifier and impair-ment. Repeat this process for MCP extension.

3. Add the flexion impairment to the exten-sion impairment to determine the total thumb impairment for decreased active motion of the MCP joint.

4. If the MCP joint is ankylosed, grade modifier 4 is used. The impairment is based on the angle of the ankylosis.

This can be considered a valid effort, and flexion impairment is rated using the maximum observed motion, 140°. 15.7d Finger Motion

The finger has 3 articular units: distal interphalan-geal (DIP) joint, proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint, and MCP joint. The actual range-of-motion measure-ments at each unit are recorded and applied for vari-ous finger impairments. These 3 units of motion have the same relative functional value as that found in amputation impairment (Table 15-31) as follows:

Distal interphalangeal joint flexion and extension: 45%. Proximal interphalangeal joint flexion and extension: 80%. Metacarpophalangeal joint flexion and extension: 100%.

Unlike the thumb, these units are not expressed using the same relative value for the denominator and, consequently, the impairment percents contrib-uted by each respective unit are combined.

Finger Distal Interphalangeal Joint: Flexion and Extension

Normal finger DIP joint motion ranges from 0° hyperextension to 70° flexion.

1. Measure the maximum flexion and extension according to Figure 15-21 and record to the nearest 10°.

2. Using the row for DIP flexion in Table 15-31, com-pare the measured greatest angle of flexion with the DIP flexion ranges in each column to establish the appropriate grade modifier and impairment. Repeat this process for DIP extension.

3. Add the flexion impairment to the exten-sion impairment to determine the total finger impairment for decreased active motion at the DIP joint.

4. If the DIP joint is ankylosed, grade modifier 4 is used. The impairment is based on the angle of the ankylosis.

Finger Proximal Interphalangeal Joint: Flexion and Extension

Normal finger PIP joint motion ranges from 0° hyperextension to 100° flexion.

1. Measure the maximum flexion and extension according to Figure 15-22.

2. Using the rows for PIP flexion and extension in Table 15-31, establish the appropriate grade modifier and impairment.

3. Add flexion and extension impairment at the PIP joint.

4. If the PIP joint is ankylosed, grade modifier 4 is used. The impairment is based on the angle of the ankylosis.

Finger Metacarpophalangeal Joint: Flexion and Extension

Normal finger MCP joint motion ranges from 20° hyperextension to 90° flexion.

1. Measure the maximum flexion and extension according to Figure 15-23.

2. Using the rows for MCP flexion and extension in Table 15-31, establish the appropriate grade modifier and impairment.

3. Add flexion and extension impairment at the MCP joint.

4. If the MCP joint is ankylosed, grade modifier 4 is used. The impairment is based on the angle of the ankylosis.

Combining Abnormal Motion at More Than One Finger Joint

If range of motion is used as a stand-alone approach to measure abnormal motion in more than 1 finger

joint, then the impairments for the affected joints are combined. Using Table 15-12, convert the digit impairment to hand impairment. Add the hand impairment values contributed by each digit to obtain the total hand impairment.

15.7e Wrist Motion Impairment

The wrist articular unit represents 60% of upper extremity function. The wrist has 2 functional units of motion as follows:

Flexion and extension: 70% wrist function (42% of upper extremity function). Radial and ulnar deviation: 30% wrist function (18% of upper extremity function).

Wrist Flexion and Extension

Normal range of wrist motion is from 60° of exten-sion to 60° of flexion. The position of function is from 10° extension to 10° flexion. The relative value of this motion unit is 42% of upper extremity function.

1. Measure the maximum flexion and extension according to Figure 15-24.

2. Using the row for wrist flexion in Table 15-32, compare the measured greatest angle of flexion with the wrist flexion ranges in each column to establish the appropriate grade and impairment. Repeat this process for wrist extension.

3. Add the upper extremity impairment for wrist flexion and extension.

4. If the wrist joint is ankylosed, grade modifier 4 is used. The impairment is based on the angle of the ankylosis.

Wrist Radial and Ulnar Deviation

Normal range of wrist motion is from 20° of radial deviation to 30°of ulnar deviation.

1. Measure the maximum radial and ulnar deviation according to Figure 15-25.

2. Using the row for wrist radial deviation in Table 15-32, compare the measured greatest angle of radial deviation with the wrist radial devia-tion ranges in each column to establish the appropriate grade and impairment rating. Repeat this process for wrist ulnar deviation.

Referencing Table 15-12 Impairment Values Calculated From Digit Impairment the thumb impairment of 36% DI equals 14% HI (hand

impairment) and the index finger impairment of 79% DI equals 16% HE. These impairments are added resulting in 30% HI. Per Table 15-11 Impairment Values Calculated From Upper Extremity Impairment this converts to 27% UEI.

Referencing Table 15-35, Range of Motion Grade Modifiers, her 27% UEI is consistent with grade modifier 3. Referencing Table 15-7 Functional History Adjustment- Upper Extremity, both her symptoms and her QuickDASH are consistent with grade modifier 3. Since her range of motion grade modifier and functional history adjustment are both the same grade modifier 3, no modification of her impairment is required per Table 15-36 Functional History Grade Adjustment: Range of Motion. Her final impairment is 27% UEI or 16% WPI.

Comment: There is no diagnosis on the finger or thumb grids which reflects the severity of her injury. Range of motion is most appropriate method to assess her impairment.

EXAMPLE 15-25: SHOULDER MOTION DEFICIT

Subject: 55-year-old woman

History: Developed an impingement syndrome related to her constant overhead work. She was treated with subacromial decompression. Following the procedure she developed a postoperative infec-tion. After 6 months of appropriate antibiotic treat-ment and physical therapy she has reached maximum medical improvement.

Current Symptoms: Complains of motion deficits that result in significant interference with activities of daily living, particularly involving work activities above shoulder level.

Functional Assessment: QuickDASH score is 60.

Physical Exam: Examination is only remarkable for her motion deficits with shoulder flexion 90°, extension 30°, abduction 83°, adduction 0°, exter-nal rotation 0° and internal rotation 12°. Motion deficits were reproducible and consistent with other documentation.

Clinical Studies: MRI revealed findings consistent with rotator cuff disease, without evidence of tear.

Diagnosis: Shoulder motion deficit, presumed sec-ondary to prolonged immobilization and infection.

Impairment Rating: Measurements are rounded up or down to the nearest number ending in 0 (per Table 15-34 Shoulder Range of Motion, flexion 90° =3% UEI; extension 30° =1% UEI; abduction 83° (rounded to 80°) =6% UEI; adduction 0° =2% UEI; internal rotation 12° (rounded to 10°) =4% UEI; external rota-tion=0° =2% UEI. Total motion deficit is obtained by adding values resulting in 18% UEI.

Referencing Table 15-35, Range of Motion Grade Modifiers, her 18% UEI is consistent with grade modifier 2. Referencing Table 15-7 Functional History Adjustment: Upper Extremity, both her symptoms and her QuickDASH are consistent with grade modifier 2. Since her Range of Motion and functional history adjustment are both the same grade modifier 2, no modification of her impair-ment is required, per Table 15-36 Functional History Grade Adjustment: Range of Motion. Her final impairment is 18% UEI or 11% WPI.

Comment: There is no diagnostic category which fits her injury and there are significant motion deficits, therefore the most appropriate rating is the range of motion. Her functional reports were consistent with other documentation and her examination. If her functional history, as defined in Table 15-7, was more severe, at level of grade modifier 3, there would have been a 1 grade differ-ence with the grade assigned to her motion deficit. In such a case, per Table 15-36 Functional History Grade Adjustment: Range of Motion her impair-ment would be increased by Total Range of Motion Impairment × 5%, ie, increased by 18% UEI × 5%, or 0.9% UEI (rounded up to 1% UEI) and would result in 19% UEI or 11% WPI.

15.8 Summary

EXAMPLE 15-26 MULTIPLE UPPER EXTREMITY IMPAIRMENTS

Subject: 57-year-old man.

History: A factory worker has a 20-year history of performing repetitive, forceful tasks, primarily involv-ing his right upper extremity. He has been an exem-plary employee and has continued to work despite a several year history of problems with discomfort in his elbow and wrist. He was diagnosed years ago as having lateral epicondylitis, and has received appro-priate conservative therapy which improved his symp-toms. Four years ago an MRI revealed a triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tear and he underwent surgical intervention with marked improvement in the pain he had been experiencing. Two years ago he was diagnosed as having a right carpal tunnel syndrome, electrodiagnostically confirmed, and he underwent a carpal tunnel release with resolution of his symptoms. One year ago he caught his right little finger in a press and the distal portion was amputated. There were no previous impairment ratings.

Current Symptoms: His only complaint of sig-nificance is his “tennis elbow” pain, and to a lesser degree occasional discomfort in his wrist. He denies any sensory difficulties or weakness. He denies any difficulties with his activities of daily living that he would attribute to his amputation.

Functional Assessment: The QuickDASH score is 21.

Physical Exam: Right little finger is amputated at the level of the distal interphalangeal joint; other-wise no observed abnormalities except very faint scars from his surgeries. Tender approximately 2 cm. distal to the lateral epicondyle in the area of the extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle. Wrist exten-sion and supination against resistance with the elbow extended increases his symptoms. Minimal tender over the TFCC and proximal palm. Range of motion is full and no neurological deficits.

Clinical Studies: Wrist and elbow X rays are unre-markable. MRI revealed a small triangular fibro-cartilage complex (TFCC) tear. Electrodiagnostic studies pre-operatively revealed mild sensory and motor conduction delays of the right median nerve.

Diagnosis: (1) Lateral epicondylitis, (2) Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tear, surgically repaired, (3) Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, resolved, s/p Carpal tunnel release, (4) Amputation little finger at DIP joint.

Impairment Rating: There are 4 ratable condi-tions. The first 2 diagnoses are rated as a Diagnosis-Based Impairment (Section 15.2). The carpal tunnel syndrome is rated by Section 15.4f, Entrapment Neuropathy and the amputation is rated by Section 15.6. Functional adjustments are applied only to the single, highest diagnosis-based impairment (DBI), which after rating was determined to be his triangu-lar fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tear.

Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tear is rated using Table 15-3, Wrist Regional Grid: Upper Extremity Impairments. Under the section “Ligament/Bone/Joint” and diagnosis “Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tear” and per criteria of “Documented TFCC injury +/− surgery with residual findings” he is assigned to class 1 with mid-range default value of 8% UEI. Adjustment Grids: Functional History: Grade modifier 1 (QuickDASH in range of 21 to 40), Physical Examination: Grade modifier 1 (Minimal palpatory findings, consistently documented, without observed abnormalities), and Clinical Tests: Grade modifier 1 (interpreted as “Clinical studies confirm diagnosis, mild pathol-ogy”). Net adjustment compared with diagnostic class is 0, resulting in grade C and remains at 8% UEI.
