When evaluating an individual with upper extremity impairment, first obtain the patient’s detailed history and perform a thorough and careful physical exami-nation; then follow these suggested steps.

1. Record process and results using the Upper

Extremity Impairment Evaluation Record (Figure 15-2).

2. Obtain detailed history and perform an appro-

priate physical examination, as explained in Section 15.1a.

3. Review clinical studies, as explained in

Section 15.1b.

4. Determine the diagnoses and those that are to be

rated.

5. Determine the DBI for each ratable diagno-

sis, using the regional grids, as explained in Sections 15.2 and 15.3.

6. Use the adjustment grids for functional his-

tory, physical examination, and clinical studies, as described in Sections 15.3a through 15.3c, to define the grade modifier for each factor. Functional history adjustment is performed only for the single most significant diagnosis, unless otherwise specifically stated by a jurisdiction.

7. Adjust the DBI, as explained in Section 15.2.

8. If there is more than 1 ratable diagnosis, com-

bine the final impairment value at the upper extremity level.

9. Identify and calculate impairment related to the

peripheral nerve impairment, as explained in Section 15.4.

10. Identify and calculate impairment related to CRPS, as explained in Section 15.5.

11. Identify and calculate impairment related to amputation, as explained in Section 15.6.

12. Only if no other approach is available to rating, calculate impairment based on range of motion, as explained in Section 15.7.

13. Typically, only a single approach is used and in nearly all cases this will be the DBI assessment; however, if multiple approaches are applicable, combine the impairments at the upper extremity level.

14. As appropriate, convert the final impairment to regional or whole person impairment.

15. If both upper extremities are involved, each extremity is rated separately and converted to whole person impairment; then both whole per-son ratings (right and left upper extremity) are combined using the Combined Values Chart.

15.9 Appendix 15-A: Functional Assessment Inventories

QuickDASH

The QuickDASH is a shortened version of the DASH (Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand). The DASH Outcome Measure and the QuickDASH are the shared property of the Institute for Work & Health (IWH) and the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS). The tools were developed by the Institute and the AAOS. The proj-ect was supported by the American Association for Hand Surgery, the American Orthopaedic Society for Sports Medicine, the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons, the American Society for Surgery of the Hand, the Arthroscopy Association of North America, and the American Society of Plastic Surgeons. The QuickDash is available at http://www.dash.iwh.on.ca/outcome_quick.htm.

The QuickDASH can be presented in 2 formats. The traditional model is with discrete integers that range from 1 to 5 (1 is not difficult, not limited, or none; 2 is mild difficulty, slightly limited, or mild; 3 is mod-erate difficulty, moderately limited, or moderate; 4 is severe difficulty, very limited, or severe; and 5 is unable, extremely, or extreme). The second format is using a visual analog scale. In this method a line that is 10 cm long is marked from 0, none, to 10, worst possible. The patient then makes a mark on the line to indicate his or her degree of difficulty in complet-ing the task. This mark is measured and rounded to the nearest centimeter, with the resulting integer being the patient’s answer. Each format has unique advantages and disadvantages. Whatever method is used, the patient’s answers to the PDQ should be dated and attached to the impairment evaluation report. For Chapter 15, either method may be used.

The QuickDASH contains 11 questions, and the Work Module contains 4 additional questions. Since impairment addresses loss of function but not work activities specifically, only the first 11 questions will be used in reference to the AMA Guides. The evalu-ator may use the Work Module’s 4 questions for addi-tional insight. If there is more than 1 QuickDASH question that is not answered or is missing, the QuickDASH cannot be calculated. Therefore, if 10 or 11 QuickDASH questions have been answered, the QuickDASH can be used to establish the “Functional Scale score” used in the evaluation of upper extrem-ity impairment. If fewer than 10 QuickDASH ques-tions have been answered, the evaluator should ask the patient to complete the unanswered questions. If for some reason the patient refuses or is unable to

complete the questions (eg, the patient has died and a theoretical rating is being calculated from medical records), the QuickDASH cannot be used.

If the QuickDASH is to be used to modify the default impairment rating, the examiner must cor-relate the information provided by the QuickDASH and a list of Activities of Daily Living (ADLs). The examiner can verify that problems exist with ADLs, by having the individual complete Table 15-37 Activities of Daily Living Questionnaire and the QuickDASH Questionnaire. The physician should record, when taking the patient’s history, which of these activities can be done without difficulty, which can still be done, but with difficulty, and which the individual says he or she is unable to perform. The physician can then look for consistency in the answers to the 2 questionnaires and in the patient’s history. Actual problems with ADLs should be easy for an individual to recall, and the answers should be consistent. Inconsistent answers suggest either symptom exaggeration or problems comprehending the questionnaires due to low proficiency in English or comorbid brain pathology (eg, head injury or dementia). In addition, individual answers should be logical. Activities such as walking should not usually be impaired by upper limb impairments.

Many of the activities listed in the Table 15-37, Activities of Daily Living Questionnaire should not logically be affected by isolated problems with 1 or both upper limbs, as depicted in Table 15-38, ADLs Questionnaire Evaluation. Answers that these activi-ties are difficult or impossible to perform, assuming the questions are understood, implies either symp-tom magnification or associated comorbidity in another body part or organ system.

Many of the activities in the Activities of Daily Living Questionnaire can be directly observed by the phy-sician to document that difficulty with the activity does exist, and to quantify the degree of difficulty. Individuals can be asked to dress and to simulate eat-ing, brushing teeth, combing hair, writing, typing, feeling, grasping, and lifting. Such ADLs as seeing, hearing, and speaking can be judged while taking the medical history. Individuals can also be asked to stand, sit, walk, climb stairs, and so forth. These activities should be unaffected by upper limb problems.

The completed ADLs Questionnaire is evaluated by comparing the individual’s answers on the question-naire to the answers to inquiries about ADL dif-ficulties when the physician takes a history from the individual. Consistency is further evaluated by the physician directly observing the individual perform specific activities listed in Table 15-37.

Another measure of the consistency of ADL dif-ficulty is to compare the answers on the Activities of Daily Living Questionnaire to the answers on the QuickDASH using Table 15-39, Comparison Between QuickDASH and ADL Questionnaires. Logically, these statements follow about the con-sistency relationship between answers to the QuickDASH Questionnaire and answers to the Activities of Daily Living Questionnaire.

The physician who is rating impairment should make allowances for comorbidity that potentially explains illogical answers. Thus, if an individual with a rota-tor cuff tear indicates difficulty walking due to the rotator cuff tear, the answer is not logical. If, how-ever, the individual also has a significant knee or hip arthritis, and bilateral upper limb impairments pre-clude the use of a cane, that patient’s answers about difficulty walking may be logical.

If an individual has multiple answers that are not logical or multiple answers that are not consistent, the QuickDASH questionnaire should not be used to assign impairment ratings. In this case, Functional History is not used as a Grade Modifier, and the only grade modifiers that can potentially be used are Physical Findings and Clinical Studies. The mini-mum impairment in that grade should be chosen to represent the final impairment.

For the upper extremity section, the selection of a self-report functional assessment measure began with development of criteria against which

established measures were compared. The most important criteria are:

• Reliability: This is the degree to which data derived are dependable. Because the functional assessment measure will be administered in many different settings, to a wide variety of indi-viduals, and may need to be administered to the same person at various times, procedures must be standardized and described in an administrator’s manual. Instructions must be understandable in the primary language of the individual. Items must be understandable in the primary language of the individual. The items must be easily interpretable from English to the individual’s native language, so that an in-person interpreter can provide an unequivocal oral interpretation. Because the functional assessment measure will be used to make important decisions, a method to identify less than a full effort responding should be built into the instrument. Because a paper and pencil mode of administration will be used, a method to accept reliable scores from incomplete data sets should be available. Because normative comparisons will be made, nonstandard modifi-cations must be discouraged. The test-retest reli-ability coefficient must be at least r = .90.

• Validity: This is the degree to which evidence and theories support the interpretation of func-tional assessment measure scores for its intended purpose: “Does the score measure what it is

intended to measure?” The functional assess-ment measure rating of severity of functional limitations must have good sensitivity and speci-ficity. The rating must represent the severity of the functional limitations at the highest level of scaling, between the ordinal and interval levels. The rating must focus on functional limitations that are caused by upper limb musculoskeletal impairment, including the fingers, hand, wrist, elbow, and shoulder. The functional assessment measure must be diagnosis-neutral, gender-neu-tral, and age-neutral. It must consider a wide range of functional abilities. The functional assessment measure must focus on the person’s ability to perform common and easily under-stood activities that have a low skill component. Items must be simple with low cognitive demand. These are more easily translated into various languages and are more likely to be within the repertoire of a broad range of individuals. Because the typical interface between the person and the activity is mediated by a tool, piece of equipment, or workstation, only those that are universally designed and used in a standard or invariant manner should be included. As much as possible, the application of the tool, equipment, or workstation should be specified to minimize ambiguity. Normative data should be available. Cross-references to widely used rating systems should be available. The information gained from

the functional assessment measure must be useful in clinical decision-making for the individual.

• Practicality: Materials must be low-cost, with easy replacement of expendable supplies. The functional assessment measure must be able to be administered by a trained clerk in 5 minutes or less, and scoring completed in 2 minutes or less. Typical interpretation by the physician must be completed in 2 minutes or less, and reports of the results in 2 minutes or less.

• Forensic Defensibility: Formal reliability and validity studies of the functional assessment mea-sure must be undertaken and published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

A number of self-report functional assessment mea-sures that address upper extremity function were considered and are listed in Table 15-40. A simple scoring rubric was used to compare the measures, assigning a value of 1 to a “should” criterion that was met and a value of 3 to a “must” criterion that was met. A total score of 66 was possible. None of the measures met all of the criteria. At this time, the QuickDASH appears to be the most acceptable functional assessment measure. This instrument addresses the criteria adequately. Although it has a few deficiencies, none are considered so serious that it cannot be recommended. On this basis, the QuickDASH has been selected as the functional assessment measure for the upper extremity section.

Appendix 15-B: Electrodiagnostic Evaluation of Entrapment Syndromes

The following criteria are to be used in interpreting electrodiagnostic testing for entrapment syndromes.

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

Conduction Delay

For carpal tunnel syndrome, or CTS (median nerve), criteria include:

• Distal motor latency longer than 4.5 milliseconds for an 8-cm study.

• Distal peak sensory latency longer than 4.0 mil-liseconds for a 14-cm distance.

• Distal peak compound nerve latency of longer than 2.4 milliseconds for a transcarpal or midpal-mar study of 8 cm.

If different distances were used in testing, correc-tion to the distances stated above can be accom-plished by assuming each 1 cm of distance requires 0.2 milliseconds.

Conduction Block

For impairment rating purposes, the definition of median nerve conduction block at the carpal tunnel is a drop in the abductor pollicis brevis (APB) com-pound motor action potential (CMAP) amplitude of at least 30% when wrist stimulation is compared with palm stimulation. Care must be taken to ensure that palm stimulation of the median nerve is supramaxi-mal and that other thenar intrinsic muscles (ulnar nerve) have not been stimulated by volume conduc-tion; the CMAP wave form should be similar in shape and should not change when stimulation intensity is increased. In many individuals the technical issues associated with this method prevent a clear diagnosis of motor conduction block in carpal tunnel syndrome.

If motor conduction block cannot be established because of technical issues, sensory conduction block on an antidromic sensory study may be present. If the 14-cm (or wrist stimulation, digit recording) sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) amplitude is reduced by 50% or more compared with the 7-cm (or palm to digit) SNAP amplitude study, sensory conduction block has been established for the purpose of impairment rating.

In bilateral studies, if the CMAP amplitude with wrist stimulation or the SNAP amplitude with antidromic wrist stimulation is 50% lower on the involved side than on the contralateral normal side, conduction block is present.

If the CMAP with wrist stimulation is below 4 mV, and the needle electromyogram (EMG) is still nor-mal, motor conduction block is present.

Axon Loss

For impairment rating purposes, axon loss is con-firmed either by needle EMG or by nerve conduction testing. In carpal tunnel syndrome, axon loss will usually be established by needle EMG findings of “denervation.” Needle EMG should show fibrillations and positive waves in the thenar eminence (APB) and will typically show at least some high amplitude and generally polyphasic motor unit potentials in chronic CTS. Recruitment must be reduced.

On nerve conduction testing, axon loss is recognized by a CMAP of less than normal (generally less than 4 mV) recorded from the APB with palm stimula-tion. Care must be taken to ensure that palm stimula-tion of the median nerve is supramaximal and that other thenar intrinsic muscles (ulnar nerve) have not been stimulated by volume conduction; the CMAP wave form should be similar in shape and should not change when stimulation intensity is increased. In many individuals the technical issues associated with this method prevent a clear diagnosis of motor axon loss by nerve conduction testing in carpal tunnel syndrome.

Ulnar Neuropathy at the Wrist (Guyon’s Canal)

Conduction Delay

For ulnar tunnel syndrome at the wrist (ulnar nerve), criteria include:

• Distal motor latency longer than 4.5 milliseconds for an 8-cm study.

• Distal peak sensory latency longer than 4.0 milliseconds for a 14-cm distance.

• Distal peak compound nerve latency longer than 2.4 milliseconds for a transcarpal or midpalmar study of 8 cm.

If different distances were used in testing, correc-tion to the distances stated above can be accom-plished by assuming each 1 cm of distance requires 0.2 milliseconds.

Conduction Block

For ulnar nerve conduction block, a drop of at least 30% in the compound muscle action potential of either the abductor digiti minimi or the first dorsal interosseous (FDI) muscle must be recorded when wrist stimulation is compared with palm stimulation.

In bilateral studies, if the CMAP amplitude with wrist stimulation or the SNAP amplitude with antidromic wrist stimulation is 50% lower on the involved side than on the contralateral normal side, conduction block is present.

Axon Loss

For impairment rating purposes, the diagnosis of axon loss is made either by needle EMG or by nerve conduction velocity. Needle EMG should show fibril-lations and positive waves in the hypothenar eminence (abductor digit minimi) or first dorsal interosseous muscle. In chronic ulnar tunnel syndrome, it will typi-cally show at least some high-amplitude polyphasic motor unit potentials. Recruitment must be reduced. On nerve conduction testing, axon loss is identified by a CMAP recorded from the abductor digiti minimi of well less than normal (generally less than 4 mV) with palm stimulation.

Ulnar Neuropathy at the Elbow (Cubital Tunnel)

Conduction Delay

Criteria for the diagnosis of ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, for the purpose of impairment rating, include motor conduction velocity less than 50 m/s for an 8- to 10-cm segment of nerve posterior to the elbow, or an above-elbow to below-elbow 8- to 10-cm segment conduction velocity that is at least 10 m/s slower than the conduction velocity in the below elbow to wrist segment.

For ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, the elbow should be positioned at 70° to 90° of flexion for measure-ment and stimulation. This position most accurately approximates surface measurements to the actual length of the nerve. Conduction velocity should be calculated for an 8- to 10-cm segment of the ulnar nerve, posterior to the elbow. Stimulation more than 3 cm distal to the medial epicondyle should be avoided, as the nerve becomes quite deep within the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle, and there is substantial risk of submaximal stimulation.

Conduction Block

For these tests, the motor recording electrode can be over either the abductor digiti minimi or the first dorsal

interosseous (FDI) muscle. Recording from the FDI muscle may increase test sensitivity. With the concomi-tant presence of conduction delay by the above criteria, a decrease in the CMAP amplitude greater than 40% when the above-elbow (across-elbow) segment is com-pared with the below-elbow segment, is consistent with motor conduction block of the ulnar nerve at the elbow. If the conduction velocity in both the above-elbow and the below-elbow ulnar nerve segments are less than 45 m/s, and the calculated conduction velocities in the median and radial nerves are all normal (greater than 50 m/s), at least ulnar nerve motor conduction block is also present by these definitions.

Axon Loss

For ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, axon loss for impairment rating purposes is usually diagnosed by the needle EMG. Denervation changes (positive waves, fibrillations, and high-amplitude polyphasic motor units) must be present in muscles innervated by the ulnar nerve distal to the site of entrapment. The FDI muscle may be the muscle most sensitive to focal ulnar neuropathy. Neither changes limited to the FDI muscle nor sparing of the forearm muscles exclude an elbow site of compromise.

Median Nerve Entrapment in the Proximal Forearm (Anterior Interosseous)

Median nerve compromise in the proximal forearm, usually at the pronator teres muscle, is uncommon. Simultaneous entrapment of the median nerve both in the carpal tunnel and at the elbow is very rare, and should be diagnosed with caution. Most often these cases are moderate carpal tunnel syndrome with proximal referral of symptoms. Conduction block of the fastest axons at the wrist may cause a delay in the calculated forearm conduction velocity.

The forearm conduction velocity is computed by recording from the APB in the palm and is thus affected by carpal tunnel syndrome. If simultaneous entrapments are suspected by both clinical examination and electrodiagnostic studies, the carpal tunnel syn-drome is usually treated with surgical release and the electrodiagnostic studies and clinical exam for symp-tom severity are repeated 6 months postoperatively. With this treatment, the “proximal entrapment” usually resolves and, therefore, was likely never present.

For the uncommon median nerve neuropathy near the elbow, nerve conduction studies may not permit the diagnosis to be made with enough certainty for impairment rating. Studies that fail to meet the defi-

nitions listed below are considered normal studies for impairment rating purposes.

Conduction Delay

A calculated forearm motor conduction velocity (stimulation just proximal to the elbow flexion crease and recording from the APB) that is less than 50 m/s while the distal motor latency (wrist to APB) is nor-mal (less than4.5 milliseconds) is consistent with a proximal lesion causing motor conduction delay. Both a prolonged distal latency with wrist stimulation and a slow forearm motor conduction velocity for the median nerve strongly suggest only carpal tunnel syndrome with conduction block of the fastest con-ducting axons. This is not usually a sign of simulta-neous carpal tunnel syndrome and proximal median nerve compression neuropathy near the elbow.

Conduction Block

With elbow stimulation and recording from the APB, a CMAP amplitude of less than 4 mV in the presence of a calculated forearm motor conduction velocity of less than 50 m/s, with a distal motor latency at the wrist of less than 4.5 milliseconds, is consistent with proximal or elbow entrapment of the median nerve, assuming that ulnar testing has excluded a congenital anastomo-sis of the median and ulnar nerves. There will usually also be significant change in the configuration of the CMAP wave form. On bilateral testing with stimula-tion just above the elbow flexion crease, a CMAP amplitude that on the involved side is 50% or less of the amplitude on the uninvolved side in either the APB or the pronator quadratus qualifies as conduction block.

Axon Loss

Denervation changes limited to muscles innervated by the median nerve distal to the elbow entrapment must be present. For compression neuropathy in the pronator teres muscle, the needle EMG should show denervation changes (fibrillation potentials and positive waves and/ or high-amplitude polyphasic potentials) in at least 2 of the distally innervated median nerve forearm muscles. These muscles are the flexor carpi radialis, flexor digi-torum sublimis, flexor digitorum profundus to digits 2 and 3, flexor pollicis longus, and the pronator quadra-tus. Abnormalities have been reported most often in the flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus to digits 2 and 3. For compression neuropathy in the dis-tal arm (at the ligament of Struthers) the needle EMG should, in addition to the just-mentioned criteria, show denervation changes (fibrillation potentials and positive waves) in the pronator teres. Needle exam changes in the ABP alone strongly suggest that carpal tunnel syn-drome is present, rather than proximal median neuropa-thy at the elbow. Nerve conduction studies should not be consistent with a generalized peripheral neuropathy,

and the needle exam should not be consistent with a more proximal lesion (plexopathy or radiculopathy). Recruitment must be reduced.

Radial Nerve Entrapment

Radial nerve entrapment near the elbow or axilla or in the spiral groove of the humerus is rare, and a suc-cessful result from surgical decompression of a “radial nerve entrapment” at the elbow (posterior interosseous nerve entrapment) in a workers’ compensation patient is even rarer. These diagnoses should be made with caution. Isolated trauma to the sensory branch, the superficial radial nerve (“hand cuff neuropathy”), is not an entrapment and should be rated from the acute peripheral nerve injury section. This pure sensory injury produces radial nerve sensory conduction slow-ing and/or SNAP amplitude loss with recording from the thumb, with a normal radial nerve motor study.

For the very uncommon radial nerve entrapment just below the elbow (posterior interosseous nerve at the supinator) bilateral studies are helpful, as this is very rarely a bilateral process. There should be a normal superficial radial nerve SNAP (greater than 7 μV) as the superficial radial nerve arises proximal to the site of compression.

Conduction Delay

Absolute calculated conduction velocities for the radial nerve are difficult to interpret, as it is difficult to accurately measure the length of the radial nerve by surface techniques. With stimulation at the elbow and recording from the extensor indicis proprius, a motor latency on the involved side that is 2 or more milliseconds longer than on the uninvolved side is consistent with motor conduction delay.

Conduction Block

In conduction block lesions, the extensor indicis pro-prius (EIP) CMAP should be normal compared with the contralateral side with stimulation in the mid-forearm (generally the normal side will be greater than 3 mV). It should be at least 30% lower with stimulation at or just above the elbow.

Axon Loss

In axon loss lesions there should be a reduced CMAP recorded from the EIP (generally less than 2 mV) and at least 30% less than the contralateral CMAP. The needle exam should show denervation changes in at least 2 of the following muscles: EIP, extensor carpi ulnaris, or extensor digitorum communis. In addition, radial nerve innervated muscles proximal to

the origin of the posterior interosseous nerve should be normal (triceps, brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus). The needle exam should not be con-sistent with a cervical radiculopathy or plexopathy, and the nerve conduction study should not be consis-tent with a generalized peripheral neuropathy.

T A B L E 1 5 - 9 ( C O N T I N U E D ) Clinical Studies Adjustment: Upper Extremities
Electrodiagnostic Testing Note: If the EMG test results meet some of, but not all of, the crite- ria for a specific class, the next lower class is the class to be used in rating the impairment
Normal
Needle EMG done at least 3 wk but less than 9 mo after injury shows at least 1 + fibrillation potentials and posi- tive waves in at least 2 muscles innervated by the injured nerve. If the EMG study is first done more than 9 mo post injury, the exam shows high- amplitude polypha- sic muscle potentials in at least 1 muscle and recruitment in that muscle is at least mildly reduced.
Needle EMG done at least 3 wk but less than 9 mo after injury shows at least 2 + fibrillation potentials and positive waves in at least 2 muscles innervated by the injured nerve. If the EMG study is first done more than 9 mo post injury, the exam shows high-amplitude polyphasic muscle potentials in at least 2 muscles and recruit- ment in those muscles is at least moderately decreased.
Needle EMG done at least 3 wk but less than 9 mo after injury shows at least 3 + fibrilla- tion potentials and positive waves in at least 3 muscles innervated by the injured nerve. If the EMG study is first done more than 9 mo post injury, the exam shows high-ampli- tude polyphasic muscle potentials in at least 3 muscles and recruitment in those muscles is severely decreased.
Needle EMG done at least 3 wk but less than 9 mo after injury shows at least 4 + fibrilla- tion potentials and positive waves in at least 3 muscles innervated by the injured nerve. If the EMG study is first done more than 9 mo post injury, the exam shows no motor units (fibrofatty replacement of muscle) in at least 2 muscles.

T A B L E 1 5 - 2 4 Diagnostic Criteria for Complex Regional Pain Syndrome
1) Continuing pain, which is disproportionate to any inciting event.
2) Must report at least 1 symptom in 3 of the 4 following categories: _____ Sensory: Reports of hyperesthesia and/or allodynia _____ Vasomotor: Reports of temperature asymmetry and/or skin color changes and/or skin color asymmetry _____ Sudomotor/Edema: Reports of edema and/or sweating changes and/or sweating asymmetry _____ Motor/Trophic: Reports of decreased range of motion and/or motor dysfunction (weakness, tremor, dystonia) and/or trophic changes (hair, nail, skin)
3) Must display at least 1 sign a at time of evaluation in 2 or more of the following categories: _____ Sensory: Evidence of hyperalgesia (to pinprick) and/or allodynia (to light touch and/or deep somatic pressure and/or joint movement) _____ Vasomotor: Evidence of temperature asymmetry and/or skin color changes and/or asymmetry _____ Sudomotor/Edema: Evidence of edema and/or sweating changes and/or sweating asymmetry _____ Motor/Trophic: Evidence of decreased range of motion and/or motor dysfunction (weakness, tremor, dystonia) and/or trophic changes (hair, nail, skin)
4) There is no other diagnosis that better explains the signs and symptoms.
a A sign is counted only if it is observed and documented at time of the impairment evaluation.
